subject: literature
passage: The tenants had sent their most reasonable man to Mr. Garrow, and Harding was reasonable: he laid out the figures, conceded every point that could honestly be conceded, and asked for nothing but a year's delay on the new rents until the drainage was repaired. Mr. Garrow heard him through with perfect civility and then declined, not angrily, but as one declines a dish one has already decided against. Harding tried the figures again, then an appeal to the old landlord's memory, then a plain request; each was received with the same courtesy and the same refusal. He went home understanding that he had been dealing not with a man who could be persuaded but with one who was ______, and whose politeness was merely the form his refusal took.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

explanation.why: The blank contrasts with "a man who could be persuaded." Garrow refuses every approach, "as one declines a dish one has already decided against," and his courtesy is only "the form his refusal took." A person who will not change position no matter what is "intransigent."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Irresolute" means unable to decide. Garrow has "already decided" and never wavers; the problem is the opposite of indecision.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Magnanimous" means generous. Garrow refuses a modest request three times; nothing about him is generous.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Obsequious" means excessively eager to please. Garrow's courtesy might suggest this, but he pleases no one; the text says his politeness was merely the form of his refusal.
explanation.D: Correct. "Intransigent" means refusing to compromise or change one's position, which fits a man who meets every argument with the same refusal.
